rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ The atom is 'totally empty'. ✅ It is mostly empty *space*, but ≈99.9% of the mass lies in the nucleus.  ·  ❌ α-particles are electrons. ✅ They are helium nuclei (+2e, ≈7300 times heavier than an electron), so electrons cannot deflect them appreciably.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: α-scattering experiment: 1909–1911; Geiger and Marsden counted ≈1 flash in 10⁴ at large angles; gold foil ≈4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick.  ·  Rutherford received the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on radioactivity.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Find r₀ for a 5.0 MeV α-particle on gold (Z = 79). **Solution:** KE = 5.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ = 8.0 × 10⁻¹³ J; r₀ = (2 × 9×10⁹ × 79 × (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)²)/(8.0 × 10⁻¹³) ≈ 4.55 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. Since r₀ is larger than the nuclear radius, the nucleus acts as a point charge and the α-particle is never captured.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ The model failed because α-particles were absorbed. ✅ Scattering itself was explained well; the model failed on stability and line spectra.  ·  ❌ Atom radius = nuclear radius. ✅ 10⁻¹⁰ m versus 10⁻¹⁵ m.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Thomson's plum-pudding model (1904) treated the atom as diffuse positive charge with electrons embedded in it and could not explain large-angle deflection of fast α-particles (He²⁺, ≈5.5 MeV). Rutherford with Geiger and Marsden (1909–1911) probed atomic *structure* by α-scattering — the experiment that established the **nuclear atom**.  ·  ### 2. Set-up

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Nuclear density is nearly the same for all nuclei because R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Describe the α-scattering experiment with a labelled diagram; list observations and conclusions.  ·  Use Maxwell's electromagnetic theory to explain why Rutherford's model could not account for atomic stability.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Quote the radiating-electron instability (collapse in ≈10⁻⁸ s) and the continuous-versus-line-spectrum defect first.  ·  Never claim Rutherford's model explained the hydrogen spectrum — repairing that was Bohr's achievement (1913).

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Radium in a lead block with a collimator gives a narrow α-beam; the target is gold foil ≈4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick (≈1000 atoms) because gold beats very thin and has a heavy nucleus (Z = 79); a rotatable ZnS screen viewed through a microscope records each scintillation; the apparatus is evacuated.  ·  ### 3. Observations  ·  • ≈99.86% of α-particles passed straight through — the atom is mostly empty space.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: State the limitations of the nuclear model and explain why Bohr's model became necessary.  ·  Calculate the distance of closest approach of a 5 MeV α-particle to a gold nucleus (Z = 79).  ·  Estimate the ratio of nuclear volume (r ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁵ m) to atomic volume (r ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) for gold.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • ≈1 in 20 000 was deflected by more than 90°, and a very few bounced back (θ ≈ 180°).  ·  • Scattering obeys N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2); large-angle scattering is rare but real.  ·  ### 4. Conclusions (nuclear model)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • Atom is neutral and largely empty; a tiny, heavy, positive **nucleus** carries almost all the mass.  ·  • Nuclear radius ≈10⁻¹⁵ m against atomic radius ≈10⁻¹⁰ m (1 : 100 000); nuclear volume ≈10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume, nuclear density ≈10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.  ·  • Electrons revolve in circular orbits, the Coulomb attraction of the nucleus giving the centripetal force.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • The positive charge is characteristic of the element — the origin of atomic number, later proved by Moseley (1913).  ·  ### 5. Quantitative results  ·  • Distance of closest approach (KE → electrostatic PE): r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m for 5 MeV α on gold — an experimental upper limit on nuclear size.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • Rutherford scattering law N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) explains why back-scattering is the rarest event.  ·  ### 6. Applications  ·  • Founded nuclear physics: led to the proton (1919) and neutron (1932) and to nuclear fission/reactor technology; Rutherford backscattering spectroscopy (RBS) still analyses thin films industrially.
